scheme.mark_scheme: Circuit: a dedicated path is set up and reserved between sender and receiver for the whole communication (1). Packet: data split into packets that travel independently, possibly by different routes, and are reassembled (1)
scheme.model_answer: Circuit switching: a dedicated path is reserved between the two devices for the whole session. Packet switching: data is split into packets that may take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

questions.title: Reassembly
questions.text: Explain how the receiver rebuilds a message sent by packet switching when the packets arrive in the order 3, 1, 4, 2.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Each packet has a sequence number in its header (1)
- the receiver waits for all packets (requests missing / damaged ones) and puts them in order 1, 2, 3, 4 using the sequence numbers (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each packet carries a sequence number, so the receiver collects all four, asks again for any missing or damaged one, and puts them back in the order 1, 2, 3, 4.

questions.title: Two differences
questions.text: Explain **two** differences between packet switching and circuit switching.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two, both sides (1 each): addresses only at set-up vs in every packet; one dedicated channel vs different routes; in order vs reassembled; reserved vs shared bandwidth; connection lost vs rerouted on failure; constant vs variable delay
scheme.model_answer: 1 In circuit switching addresses are needed only to set up the connection, whereas in packet switching every packet carries the sender and receiver addresses. 2 Circuit switching sends all data along one reserved channel in order, whereas packets can take different routes and are reassembled.

questions.title: Online classes
questions.text: A university conducts online classes for students. Data is transmitted using packet switching. State **two** problems that can arise.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): picture and sound not synchronised; interruptions / video not continuous / freezing; degraded by other competing traffic; lost packets → poor quality

questions.title: A link fails
questions.text: Explain what happens to the communication when one link of the network fails during (a) a circuit-switched call and (b) a packet-switched transfer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Circuit: the reserved path is broken so the connection / call is lost and must be set up again (1); Packet: routers send the following packets along another route, the transfer continues / lost packets are resent (1)
scheme.model_answer: (a) The dedicated path is broken, so the call is cut off. (b) Routers simply send the remaining packets another way and any lost packets are resent.

Packets always take the shortest route

scheme.mark_scheme:
- MAC addresses identify the next device on the local link / deliver frames within a LAN (switches use them) (1)
- they change at each hop while the IP addresses stay the same (1)
scheme.model_answer: MAC addresses deliver the frame to the next device on the local link, such as the router or the destination computer; they change at every hop while the source and destination IP addresses stay the same.

questions.title: At each hop

questions.title: ARP

scheme.mark_scheme:
- It sends an ARP request broadcast to all devices on the LAN asking who has that IP (1)
- the router replies with its MAC address (1)
- the computer stores it in its ARP cache and uses it in the frame header (1)
scheme.model_answer: The computer broadcasts an ARP request "Who has 192.168.1.1?"; the router answers with its MAC address, which the computer stores in its ARP cache and puts in the frames it sends.

questions.title: Switching methods

parts.title: Steps
parts.text: Describe how an e-mail is sent from one computer to another using packet switching.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): message split into packets; header with source / destination IP and sequence number; routers read destination IP and forward each packet; packets may take different routes / arrive out of order; receiver checks for errors / requests missing packets; packets reassembled in order
scheme.model_answer: The e-mail is split into packets, each with the source and destination IP addresses and a sequence number. Routers forward each packet on the best route available, so they may travel different ways. The receiver checks them, asks for any missing ones and reassembles the e-mail using the sequence numbers.

questions.title: Addresses on the journey

scheme.model_answer: 1 A MAC address is a physical address set by the manufacturer, while an IP address is a network address given when the device joins a network. 2 The MAC address identifies the device's network card, while the IP address identifies where the device is on the network.

parts.title: What changes

scheme.mark_scheme: Destination IP 185.22.66.10 stays the same for the whole journey (1); MAC addresses change at each hop (1); destination MAC is always the next router / finally the server; source MAC is the device sending on that link (1)
scheme.model_answer: The destination IP address 185.22.66.10 stays the same. The MAC addresses change at every hop: each frame is addressed from the device sending it to the next router, and on the last link to the web server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): links shared → more users / efficient use of bandwidth; rerouting around failures → reliable; no set-up time; cheaper; only lost packets resent; one network for voice and data
scheme.model_answer: 1 Links are shared by many users, so more customers are served with the same cables. 2 If a link fails, packets are rerouted, so service continues. 3 One network carries both calls and Internet data, which is cheaper.

parts.title: Disadvantages
parts.text: Explain **two** disadvantages of packet switching for voice calls.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): variable delay / jitter → speech breaks up; packets out of order / lost → gaps in speech; quality drops when network congested; header overhead

scheme.mark_scheme: Packets travel across shared networks / routers owned by others (1); could be intercepted, encryption makes them unreadable (1)
scheme.model_answer: Packets cross shared networks where they could be intercepted; encryption means anyone capturing them cannot understand the call.

scheme.mark_scheme: The circuit is reserved for the whole call (1); even during silence no other user can use it (1)
scheme.model_answer: The whole circuit was reserved for the call, so during pauses the capacity stayed unused and no one else could use it.

summary: How networks move data by switching — circuit switching (set-up, transfer, release) and packet switching (packets, headers, independent routes, reassembly) compared with their advantages, disadvantages and problems for live video; the role of MAC and IP addresses at each hop and ARP; the format of a MAC address and ways to find the MAC address of a computer.

blocks.content: A large network such as the telephone system or the Internet does not have a direct cable between every pair of devices. Data passes through many **switching nodes** (exchanges, switches, routers). **Switching** is the method used to decide **how** data is passed through these nodes from the sender to the receiver.

items.title: Circuit switching
items.content: A **dedicated path (circuit)** is set up between sender and receiver **before** communication starts and is **reserved** for the whole session. All data follows the **same route**, in order. *Example: the traditional landline telephone network.*

items.title: Packet switching
items.content: Data is split into **packets**, each with a **header** (source and destination addresses, sequence number). Packets travel **independently**, possibly by **different routes**, and are **reassembled** in order at the destination. *Example: the Internet.*

blocks.title: The three phases of circuit switching
items: **Circuit establishment** — the sender requests a connection; each exchange on the way reserves a channel until a complete path to the receiver exists (the phone rings).
**Data transfer** — all data travels along the reserved path, **in order**, with a **constant delay**. The full bandwidth of the circuit belongs to this connection, even during silence.
**Circuit release (disconnection)** — when the call ends the path is released and the channels can be used by others.

blocks.content:
Phone A ══ Exchange 1 ══ Exchange 3 ══ Exchange 4 ══ Phone B     ← reserved circuit
                 │              │
             Exchange 2 ── Exchange 5                              ← not used by this call
blocks.caption: Circuit switching: one reserved path for the whole call

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- **Guaranteed bandwidth** — the line is not shared during the call.
- **Constant, low delay** after set-up — ideal for real-time voice.
- Data always arrives **in order**; no reassembly needed.
- Addresses are needed **only** when the connection is set up.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- **Set-up time** before any data can be sent.
- **Wastes bandwidth** — the circuit is reserved even when nobody speaks.
- If any link on the path **fails**, the connection is **lost**.
- Fewer users can be served at once — expensive for long distances.

blocks.title: Structure of a packet
rows: **Source** and **destination IP addresses**, **sequence (packet) number**, total number of packets, protocol, time to live
A piece of the actual data (e.g. 1500 bytes)

blocks.title: Packet switching step by step
items: The message is split into **packets**; each gets a **header** with source IP, destination IP, **sequence number**, packet count and a **checksum**.
Each packet is sent to the first **router**. Every router reads the **destination IP** and forwards the packet along the **best route available at that moment** (a **hop**).
Packets of the same message may take **different routes** and arrive **out of order**; some may be delayed, lost or damaged.
The receiver checks each packet with the checksum, **reorders** them using the sequence numbers and requests **missing or damaged** packets again.
When all packets have arrived, the original message is **reassembled**.

blocks.content:
┌── R2 ── R4 ──┐
  Sender ── R1             R6 ── Receiver     packet 1: R1 → R2 → R4 → R6
            └── R3 ── R5 ──┘                  packet 2: R1 → R3 → R5 → R6
                                              packet 3: R1 → R2 → R5 → R6
  Arrival order: 2, 1, 3 → reassembled as 1, 2, 3 using the sequence numbers
blocks.caption: Packet switching: packets of one message take different routes

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- **Efficient** — links are **shared** by many users; no capacity is wasted during silence.
- **Reliable** — if a router or link fails, packets are **rerouted** around it.
- No set-up time — data can be sent **immediately**.
- Lost or damaged packets are **resent individually**, not the whole message.
- Suitable for **many simultaneous users** — cheaper.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- **Variable delay** (packets queue at busy routers) — **jitter**.
- Packets can **arrive out of order** and must be reassembled — extra processing.
- Packets can be **lost** during congestion.
- Every packet carries a header — **overhead**.
- Data travels over shared networks — **encryption** needed for security.

blocks.content: In a **video lesson** sent by packet switching: picture and sound may be **not synchronised**, the video may **freeze or stutter** (packets delayed or lost), and quality may **drop** when other traffic competes for the same links. Streaming services use **buffering** and protocols that skip late packets to reduce these effects.

blocks.title: Circuit switching vs packet switching
rows: Needed only to set up the connection
**Every packet** carries source and destination addresses
May arrive out of order — reassembled using sequence numbers
Constant, low after set-up — good for real-time voice
Packets are rerouted around the failure
Packets cross shared networks — encryption needed

items.title: Two kinds of address work together
items.content:
- **IP addresses** get a packet to the right **network** — **routers** use them to move packets **between networks**.
- **MAC addresses** get the frame to the right **device** on the **local link** — **switches** and network cards use them.

items.title: What changes at each hop
items.content:
- The **packet's** source and destination **IP addresses stay the same** for the whole journey.
- The **frame's MAC addresses change** at every hop: the source is the device sending on this link, the destination is the **next** device (a router, or finally the receiver).

blocks.title: A packet from a laptop to a web server
blocks.content:
| Hop | Source MAC → destination MAC | Source IP → destination IP |
|---|---|---|
| Laptop → school router | Laptop → **school router** | 192.168.1.25 → 185.22.66.10 |
| School router → ISP router | School router → **ISP router** | (public address after NAT) → 185.22.66.10 |
| Last router → web server | Last router → **web server** | … → 185.22.66.10 |

The destination **IP** never changes; the destination **MAC** is always the **next stop**.

blocks.title: ARP — finding the MAC address for an IP address
items: A device knows the **IP address** it wants to reach on its LAN (the router or another computer) but not its **MAC address**.
It sends an **ARP request** to **all** devices on the LAN (broadcast): "Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.25."
The device with that IP replies with its **MAC address** (ARP reply).
The sender stores the pair in its **ARP cache** and uses the MAC address in the frame header.

blocks.title: MAC address format
rows: Last 24 bits — unique number of the **network card**
Pairs separated by colons `3C:52:82:1A:9F:04` or hyphens `3C-52-82-1A-9F-04`

theory.title: Finding the MAC address of a computer

blocks.title: Ways to find the MAC address
rows: *Control Panel → Network and Internet → Network and Sharing Center → View network status and tasks →* adapter → **Details**
*Device Manager → Network adapters →* properties of the NIC
`ifconfig en0` in Terminal, or *System Settings → Network → Details*

blocks.content:
Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi:
   Description . . . . . . . . . . . : Intel(R) Wi-Fi 6 AX201
   Physical Address. . . . . . . . . : 3C-52-82-1A-9F-04
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.25
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
blocks.caption: Part of the output of ipconfig /all

blocks.content: Phones and laptops may use a **randomised (private) MAC address** for each Wi-Fi network to protect privacy, so the address shown for a network can differ from the hardware address. A computer with both Wi-Fi and Ethernet has **two** MAC addresses — one per network card.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain two differences between packet switching and circuit switching. [2]**
In circuit switching the addresses are only needed when the connection is **set up**, whereas in packet switching **each packet** carries the sender and receiver addresses (1). Circuit switching delivers data **in order along one reserved channel**, whereas in packet switching packets can take **different routes** and are reassembled (1).

**Q: State two problems that can arise when an online class uses packet switching. [2]**
Picture and sound may be **not synchronised** (1); the video may be **interrupted / not continuous** or degraded by competing traffic (1).

**Q: Write two ways to identify the MAC address of a computer. [2]**
Using the **command prompt** with `ipconfig /all` (1); through **Control Panel → Network and Internet → View network status → adapter Details** / NIC properties (1).

**Q: Describe the role of MAC addresses in packet routing. [2]**
MAC addresses identify the **next device on the local link** so frames reach the right router or computer (1); they **change at each hop**, while the IP addresses stay the same (1).

- Saying packet switching "sets up a route first" — that is **circuit switching**.
- Saying packets always arrive in order — they can arrive **out of order**.
- Saying MAC addresses are used to route across the Internet — routers use **IP** addresses; MAC is for the **local link**.
- Giving one-sided differences — mention **both** methods.
